An advantage of electronic storage is that the consumer is freed from the burden of carrying paper coupons. A further advantage is that the electronic coupons may be retrieved from any location. In some embodiments, the system can track coupon expiration dates, alert the consumer about coupons that will expire soon, and/or delete expired coupons from storage. An advantage for the issuer of the coupons is the possibility of receiving more feedback about who is using the coupons and when and where they are captured and used.
    19. General Applications
    19.1. Forms
    The system may be used to auto-populate an electronic document that corresponds to a paper form. A user scans in some text or a barcode that uniquely identifies the paper form. The scanner communicates the identity of the form and information identifying the user to a nearby computer. The nearby computer has an Internet connection. The nearby computer can access a first database of forms and a second database having information about the user of the scanner (such as a service provider's subscriber information database). The nearby computer accesses an electronic version of the paper form from the first database and auto-populates the fields of the form from the user's information obtained from the second database. The nearby computer then emails the completed form to the intended recipient. Alternatively, the computer could print the completed form on a nearby printer.
    Rather than access an external database, in some embodiments, the system has a portable scanner that contains the user's information, such as in an identity module, SIM, or security card. The scanner provides information identifying the form to the nearby PC. The nearby PC accesses the electronic form and queries the scanner for any necessary information to fill out the form.
    19.2. Business Cards
    The system can be used to automatically populate electronic address books or other contact lists from paper documents. For example, upon receiving a new acquaintance's business card, a user can capture an image of the card with his/her cellular phone. The system will locate an electronic copy of the card, which can be used to update the cellular phone's onboard address book with the new acquaintance's contact information. The electronic copy may contain more information about the new acquaintance than can be squeezed onto a business card. Further, the onboard address book may also store a link to the electronic copy such that any changes to the electronic copy will be automatically updated in the cell phone's address book. In this example, the business card optionally includes a symbol or text that indicates the existence of an electronic copy. If no electronic copy exists, the cellular phone can use OCR and knowledge of standard business card formats to fill out an entry in the address book for the new acquaintance. Symbols may also aid in the process of extracting information directly from the image. For example, a phone icon next to the phone number on the business card can be recognized to determine the location of the phone number.
    19.3. Proofreading/Editing
    The system can enhance the proofreading and editing process. One way the system can enhance the editing process is by linking the editor's interactions with a paper document to its electronic counterpart. As an editor reads a paper document and scans various parts of the document, the system will make the appropriate annotations or edits to an electronic counterpart of the paper document. For example, if the editor scans a portion of text and makes the “new paragraph” control gesture with the scanner, a computer in communication with the scanner would insert a “new paragraph” break at the location of the scanned text in the electronic copy of the document.
    19.4. Voice Annotation
    A user can make voice annotations to a document by scanning a portion of text from the document and then making a voice recording that is associated with the scanned text. In some embodiments, the scanner has a microphone to record the user's verbal annotations. After the verbal annotations are recorded, the system identifies the document from which the text was scanned, locates the scanned text within the document, and attaches the voice annotation at that point. In some embodiments, the system converts the speech to text and attaches the annotation as a textual comment.
    In some embodiments, the system keeps annotations separate from the document, with only a reference to the annotation kept with the document. The annotations then become an annotation markup layer to the document for a specific subscriber or group of users.
    In some embodiments, for each capture and associated annotation, the system identifies the document, opens it using a software package, scrolls to the location of the scan and plays the voice annotation. The user can then interact with a document while referring to voice annotations, suggested changes or other comments recorded either by themselves or by somebody else.
    19.5. Help in Text
    The described system can be used to enhance paper documents with electronic help menus. In some embodiments, a markup layer associated with a paper document contains help menu information for the document. For example, when a user scans text from a certain portion of the document, the system checks the markup associated with the document and presents a help menu to the user. The help menu is presented on a display on the scanner or on an associated nearby display.
    19.6. Use with Displays
    In some situations, it is advantageous to be able to scan information from a television, computer monitor, or other similar display. In some embodiments, the portable scanner is used to scan information from computer monitors and televisions. In some embodiments, the portable optical scanner has an illumination sensor that is optimized to work with traditional cathode ray tube (CRT) display techniques such as rasterizing, screen blanking, etc.
    A voice capture device which operates by capturing audio of the user reading text from a document will typically work regardless of whether that document is on paper, on a display, or on some other medium.
    19.6.1. Public Kiosks and Dynamic Session IDs
    One use of the direct scanning of displays is the association of devices as described in Section 15.6. For example, in some embodiments, a public kiosk displays a dynamic session ID on its monitor. The kiosk is connected to a communication network such as the Internet or a corporate intranet. The session ID changes periodically but at least every time that the kiosk is used so that a new session ID is displayed to every user. To use the kiosk, the subscriber scans in the session ID displayed on the kiosk; by scanning the session ID, the user tells the system that he wishes to temporarily associate the kiosk with his scanner for the delivery of content resulting from scans of printed documents or from the kiosk screen itself. The scanner may communicate the Session ID and other information authenticating the scanner (such as a serial number, account number, or other identifying information) directly to the system. For example, the scanner can communicate directly (where “directly” means without passing the message through the kiosk) with the system by sending the session initiation message through the user's cell phone (which is paired with the user's scanner via Bluetooth™). Alternatively, the scanner can establish a wireless link with the kiosk and use the kiosk's communication link by transferring the session initiation information to the kiosk (perhaps via short range RF such as Bluetooth™, etc.); in response, the kiosk sends the session initiation information to the system via its Internet connection.
    The system can prevent others from using a device that is already associated with a scanner during the period (or session) in which the device is associated with the scanner. This feature is useful to prevent others from using a public kiosk before another person's session has ended. As an example of this concept related to use of a computer at an Internet cafe, the user scans a barcode on a monitor of a PC which s/he desires to use; in response, the system sends a session ID to the monitor that it displays; the user initiates the session by scanning the session ID from the monitor (or entering it via a keypad or touch screen or microphone on the portable scanner); and the system associates in its databases the session ID with the serial number (or other identifier that uniquely identifies the user's scanner) of his/her scanner so another scanner cannot scan the session ID and use the monitor during his/her session. The scanner is in communication (through wireless link such as Bluetooth™, a hardwired link such as a docking station, etc.) with a PC associated with the monitor or is in direct (i.e., w/o going through the PC) communication with the system via another means such as a cellular phone, etc.
    Part IV—System Details
    The term “markup” is used in a variety of ways, so it is important to clarify the sense in which it is used here. This discussion is not about “marking things up” in the sense of proof-reading, though this system can be used for that (discussed below). It concerns markup in the sense of markup languages, such as SGML, HTML, XML and stylesheet languages such as CSS, which provide a means for adding extra material to a document beyond what is immediately intended for reading by a user.
    In SGML and XML, markup is often semantic information relating to the text, or a structural framework for the text of the document.
    In HTML, markup also often adds functionality, the most obvious being the hyperlink, which provides the user with a convenient means to access other related information by clicking on the text.
    In CSS, markup typically specifies a recommended formatting of the text, for example the placement of an item on the page, background images for particular areas, and also the display or hiding of certain content based on user activity such as mouse movements.
    One way to think of the markup is as an “overlay” on the document, which provides further information about—and may specify actions associated with—the document or some portion of it. Several layers of markup may be used in conjunction with any document.
    The system uses markup in association with rendered documents, such as books, newspapers or magazine articles. Rendered documents are not in electronic form and hence cannot directly benefit from the functionality of traditional electronic markup, but the system can associate them with such electronic markup and thus enhance them in many ways.
    The system uses markup as applied to information derived from scans (optical, voice, etc.) occurring in a rendered version of a document. In some embodiments, the markup described is applied to the digital counterpart document with which the markup may be associated. In some embodiments, markup is independent of a particular document, and can be applied by the system to scanned data without locating, retrieving, or referring to the digital counterpart of the document being scanned.
    Why Markup?
    The term “markup” is often used to distinguish the content of a document, generally intended for viewing by a user, from information about the content. The term “markup” as used here specifies the latter.
    As will be explained, the markup may be embedded in a document but will often be stored separately from the document and can be created and modified without editing the document itself. This can be particularly significant where the primary document with which the user is interacting is not in electronic form. Additionally, markup data and processes can be independent of any specific document, and can instead be associated with a group of documents, class of documents, all documents, scans having certain features, etc.
    An Example Use of Markup
    The following describes the system's use of markup in some embodiments:
    A user captures some text from a paper document using a handheld scanner device. Either immediately, or later, the system processes this capture, and may use it to locate the electronic counterpart of the paper document, for example on the publisher's web site. In some cases, the system retrieves the document and examines any markup embedded in it. This may include other forms of markup that are not specific to the system, such as HTML hyperlinks.
    In this example, the electronic counterpart references a markup file which is available from the publisher's website. The system downloads it. The system also loads any markup created by the user for this document or related documents—for example, annotations made in the past.
    The system performs a web search for markup appropriate to the document, and downloads it The system connects to markup services to which the user has subscribed and requests anything appropriate to the document The system considers other material in the user's archive and automatically constructs markup which cross-references this document to others The system considers markup added to this document by other users, such as annotations   

    In some embodiments, the above operations all happen in parallel.
    The system presents the electronic document to the user, scrolled to the location of the capture, with the captured area of text highlighted. The display of the document—or sections of the document—may be modified by the markup.
    Some of the markup may add extra hypertext links to the text, for example by linking certain words and phrases to a glossary. The user can follow these links in the normal way.
    In some embodiments, the system provides further markup-originated functionality, such as in a drop-down menu revealed by right-clicking with the mouse.
    All of the above may happen on the capture device that performs the capture immediately at the time the capture occurs, that is, while the user is interacting with the paper document. In this way, a large amount of electronic functionality is effectively added directly to the paper document.
    The following sections consider common types of markup, sources from which it may be obtained, some examples of how it may be used and ways in which it may be associated with, or “attached,” to the document.
    Types of Markup
    Examples of the possible types of markup include:
    display stylesheets, which affect the electronic rendering of a document metadata, which is information about the document itself or parts of the document—for example, information about the origins of a document, its edit history, copyright and licensing notices, keywords and subject classifications semantic information about parts of the document—indicating, for example, “this is a quotation,” “this is a heading,” “this is a footnote” extra material—for example bibliographic information or further context for quoted passages, translations, explanatory movies and audio, referenced other works, online discussion forums, executive summaries instructions to the system—for example, “this document is best viewed with Acrobat Reader 6” programs—code which adds interactivity, for example, in the way that JavaScript often does in web pages links or other references to any of the above Further examples of these different types are provided later.   

    Sources of Markup
    Just as markup may be of several different types, as described above, so may it be created by and obtained from any of several sources.
    Markup Creators
    Markup may be created entirely by humans, or created entirely by machine, or come from any combination of the two. Examples of the possible creators of markup for a particular document include but are not limited to:
    The author or creator of the document The publisher or distributor of the document The user Other users Markup services. These may be free or commercial, installed on the local machine or located on the network, and will typically be installed or subscribed to by the user or the user's organization, or the publisher of the document. Advertisers Commentators and critics   

    Ways of Locating and Retrieving Markup
    Markup may be located in several ways, for example:
    it can be embedded in the original document it can be referenced in the electronic document (e.g., by URL) it can come from a standard location (e.g., from a URL that can be deduced from the document's URL) it can be found in the user's own markup database it can come from applications installed by the user it can come from a service to which somebody—for example, the publisher, the user, the user's employer, the owner of the rendered document—is subscribed it can be found by a search engine; this may be the same engine that originally located the document, or a different one and may be found as part of the same process, or separately   

    A typical use of the system involves markup being retrieved from several of these locations.
    Markup Association
    The various types of markup have been discussed, as have examples of who or what may create it, and where it may be found. This section discusses how markup may be associated with the document text.
    Markup may be associated with any body of text. A particular collection of markup, for example, may be relevant to everything on a particular company's website, or just one document, or just one section of a document, or just a paragraph, sentence or word.
    Identification of Documents
    In some embodiments, a set of rules is evaluated by the system for each collection of markup identified, to see to which bodies of text it may be applied. At the document level, an example implementation tries to match the URL of the document against each of a set of patterns (such as regular expressions) in order. Each pattern has an associated value indicating whether the markup should or should not be applied to documents matching the pattern.
    In some embodiments, markup found at one level in a filesystem or URL hierarchy is deemed to apply to all documents that are lower in the hierarchy unless overridden at a lower level. For example, the file located at:
    http://www.example.com/news/budget.html

may automatically have the markup at
 http://www.example.com/markup.xml

applied to it, unless it is overridden by the existence of markup at
 http://www.example.com/news/markup.xml

or
 http://www.example.com/news/budget.html/markup.xml   

    Markup may be directed by an almost infinite variety of criteria. Markup may be designated as applying to documents in French, to documents that are semantically similar to a particular document, to documents from a certain publication, to documents containing certain search words, to versions of a particular document modified after a certain date.
    In some embodiments, any text may have one or more separate classifications applied to it specifically to identify the nature of the text for the purposes of markup, independent of its location. As an example, a particular article in a newspaper may be tagged in its electronic version as being in category:
    news/newspaper article/financial news/international
    Rules similar to those described for URLs above may be applied to these classifications.
    Such examples need not apply purely at the document level, but also to sections of text within a document.
    Specification of Location within a Document
    In some embodiments, the system locates a file that contains markup, deems it to be applicable to a given document using the methods described above, and retrieves it. The markup contained within it may be applicable to the document as a whole, but often it will contain markup that is specific to a particular piece of text within the document. For example, it may contain more information about the source of a quotation on the third page.
    Within a document, the rules used to identify the parts of the document to which a particular item of markup should be applied may differ depending on the type of document. The specification may be as simple as “The text beginning at character 1432 and ending at character 1528.”
    In some embodiments, the system uses location descriptions that depend more on the structure of the document, thus increasing the likelihood that the location will still be valid after the document has been edited. Parts of XML documents, for example, may be identified using the XPath/XQuery syntax. This allows, for example, the specification of “All paragraphs in ‘caption’ format,” or “The paragraph in ‘caption’ format after the third table.”
    In some embodiments, the system identifies a location in terms of the textual content of the document. The specification then becomes, for example, The sentence containing the text “traveling to Cambridge on Monday morning” or “All occurrences of the text The Merchant of Venice.” In some cases, the text referred to will be the text captured from the rendered document.
    In certain situations, the system uses markup that is not directly associated with the text captured by the user in some embodiments. For example, markup may be used that is associated with phrases in the same vicinity, or markup from similar words or phrases elsewhere in the document. This use of related markup can be beneficial where user is capturing text from a paragraph not because he is only interested in the captured words, but because he is interested in the paragraph or page on which it occurs.
    In situations where the system has access to sufficient knowledge about the layout of the rendered document the system specifies, the markup in terms of this layout in some embodiments. For example, the system may associate markup with “the top half of page 13.”
    In some embodiments, where the system presents the markup to the user in the form of a popup menu, the presentation within that menu may be affected by both the specificity of the markup—that associated with the exact phrase being given more prominence than that associated with the paragraph—and the proximity—markup associated with a phrase on the previous line being given higher priority than that associated with a phrase several lines before.
    Keywords, Logos, Trademarks, Key Phrases
    Some items in documents may have particular markup associated with them based on their own characteristics rather than their location in any particular document (see Section 5.2). Examples include special marks that are printed in the document purely for the purpose of being scanned (see Section 7.3), as well as logos and trademarks that can link the user to further information about the organization concerned. The same applies to “keywords” or “key phrases” in the text. Organizations might register particular phrases with which they are associated, or with which they would like to be associated, and attach certain markup to them that would be available wherever that phrase was scanned.
    In some embodiments, the system implements such location-independent markup using “global” markup specifications, which are loaded by the system and applied to all captures that it handles.
    Examples of Use
    Earlier sections have discussed the types of markup, how markup may be created, located and associated with documents or parts of documents. This section considers some example uses to which the system can put markup.
    Cross-referencing and Hyperlinking
    Much of the power of electronic documents on the World Wide Web and similar systems comes from hyperlinks: the ability to jump from one document to another based on a particular topic of interest, the ability to choose between skimming through an article or exploring a subject in more depth, the ability quickly to locate other material to which the document refers.
    The system adds the same facility to rendered documents. In one example, printouts of web pages may be endowed with the same hyperlink functionality as their electronic counterparts. By capturing text which has a hyperlink associated with it, the user is presented with the content which is the target of the link, either at the time of capture or later, depending on the facilities available.
    In some embodiments, this process occurs entirely in the paper-based world. When reading a document, for example, a user scans a phrase that refers to another article, and that article is printed out on a nearby printer.
    Glossaries
    Capturing a particular word or phrase may cause an explanation of that word or phrase to be presented to the user. This may take the form of simple dictionary definitions, or more detailed encyclopedia-type entries, and is particularly valuable, for example, for readers of books incorporating archaic terms, nautical expressions, legal phrases or technical terminology.
    Bibliographies and Footnotes
    Many documents contain footnotes, endnotes and bibliographies, which inform the reader of the sources of quotes, the details of citations, suggested further reading. Not only can the system endow such items with hyperlinking abilities as mentioned above to make the referenced materials easier for the user to find, retrieve or purchase, but it can add extra such items to the document through the medium of markup, including after the time of publication of the document.
    Commentary
    Another example of markup use is in providing commentary on the text, such as that found in literary analysis. In some embodiments, a user reading a work of literature or other significance captures some text and is presented with commentary on the text by an expert in the field. The commentary may come from any of the sources discussed above.
    Annotation
    Users may annotate documents for their own information or for the use of others. Such annotations may be textual, but they may involve other media, including photographs, speech or other audio (see Section 19.4), or video.
    Proof-reading Marks
    One example of annotation is that used in proof-reading a document. (See Section 19.3) Many people who need to correct, edit or otherwise comment on a document will do so in its paper form, either because that is what they have been given or because they prefer reading on paper to reading on a computer display.
    Use of the system allows the reader's comments about particular words or passages to be associated with those passages while he interacts with the paper document, and yet be transmitted to the person receiving such comments in such a form that they may easily be associated with the relevant point in the electronic original, and any corrections or other changes be applied accordingly.
    Some examples of ways in which such “proof-reading” annotations may be recorded include a voice recording, a scan of some hand-written notes or symbols, or suggestions entered using the facilities of the capture device, for example with gestures (see Section 12.1.3), buttons or menu items on the device, or entered with a keyboard or keypad.
    In some embodiments, a capture device intended specifically for use in proofreading has user-interface components providing convenient access to the more common annotations. For example, buttons might be pressed immediately after a capture from the text to indicate “delete,” “rephrase,” or “rethink punctuation.”
    The proof-reading comments may, of course, be edited by the proof-reader, such as on a PC, before being sent to the final recipient.
    Translation
    In some embodiments, the system uses markup to provide a translation of text from one language to another, such as explanations of Latin phrases that appear in an otherwise English text.
    Real-time Data
    In some embodiments, the system uses markup to add to a static paper document, dynamic information dependent upon the time at which the document is consulted. Examples include current stock prices of companies mentioned in a newspaper article, current meteorological information about places referred to, or the current prices of products described in a review.
    Specific to User Context
    Other information in the markup may be dependent on the user's context at the time of the capture, or at the time of making use of the capture, or at the time of interacting with the electronic counterpart.
    For example, if the location of the reader is known, the system may provide geographically-specific information. While reading about a product, such as an unusual ingredient in a cooking recipe, the user could scan the text and be informed about nearby places where that product could be purchased. In some embodiments, when the user captures information about a place, the system presents the user with travel information specific to that place: “How to get there from here . . . ”
    In some embodiments, the system uses the time at which the user performs the capture. For example, while reading a newspaper article, the user may capture some text from it and be informed by the system of a television program on that subject which starts in half an hour. While reading about a play, the user may be told by the system about current and upcoming performances of the play in nearby theaters.
    Other examples of context may be found in section (see Section 13).
    Version Information
    In some embodiments, the system uses markup to present information about the version of the document that they user is handling. For example:
    “This document last updated on . . . by . . . ” “This section last edited by . . . ” “This version now superseded”   

    In addition, the system may tell a user capturing some text how that text has changed in the document's version history.
    “This section does not appear in versions of this document published since March 2004”   

    Multimedia Supplementary Material
    Further information associated with a document may be in the form of other media, such as audio or video.
    Example embodiments include:
    When reading a script for a play, film, or radio program, the user scans some text from the script and is presented with a presentation of the audio or video of a performance of the play, film or radio program around the point that was scanned. A person reading a newspaper sees an advertisement for a movie playing at a local cinema. He scans text from the advertisement and is shown the trailer for the movie. A student reading a textbook scans some text, and is shown the video of a lecture where a professor explains the subject scanned. (See Section 17.5). A user in the midst of reading a novel needs to leave for his drive to work. He gets into his car, scans the text of the novel where he finished reading and the audio-book version in his car starts playing from that point   

    In all of these examples, the markup associated with the captured text identifies the source of multimedia data appropriate for the text and (optionally) the part of that multimedia data from which playback should commence and where it should end.
    In some circumstances, the captured data will not be text. In some embodiments, when a user scans a few bars from a musical score, the system plays the corresponding section from a recording of a performance. (See Section 17.3.)
    In some embodiments, the system also uses markup associated with a rendered document directly to control the playback of some media. This may involve capturing text or symbols which mean “stop,” “rewind,” “play” etc., or it may involve scanning the name of a track from a CD album cover while the CD is playing causes the CD playback to jump to that track.
    Initiating or Confirming Actions
    The hyperlinks described above are not, of course, limited to the retrieval of other material. They may perform any of the operations that hyperlinks perform in other environments such as the World Wide Web. This includes sending messages, completing forms, initiating or confirming purchases, registering for email newsletters, performing calculations, submitting search queries, downloading or installing software.
    Controlling the Viewing Software
    In some embodiments, markup is generated with the knowledge of the software that is likely to be used for interacting with the electronic counterpart of the rendered document. The markup can therefore include information or instructions appropriate to that software. The markup may also specify the software to be used.
    In the example of a rendered document that originates from a Microsoft Word document, certain markup could include macros that cause Word to act in particular ways. Such markup may cause Word to display the document in a particular viewing mode, for example, or to scroll to, highlight or otherwise manipulate a particular piece of text, or to print the page on which it occurs.
    In another example, where the appropriate viewing software is a web browser, the markup may incorporate Javascript code for performing such activities in the context of the browser.
    Other Uses of the Markup
    In some embodiments, the captures made by a user are stored in an archive. The system can therefore apply markup to captures made in the past. (See Sections 6.1 and 16.1). In some cases new or modified markup may have become available since the time that the capture was performed, thereby providing more options to the user.
    In some embodiments, the system can also make markup available in normal interactions with the electronic documents. For example, markup may be consulted and used to influence the user's experience when encountering those documents on the World Wide Web.
    In some embodiments, markup can be added to the rendered document without necessarily adding it to the electronic version. This may be desirable where the markup is only relevant to possessors of the rendered document, or where older versions of the rendered document are known still to be in circulation while the electronic versions have been updated may also be used as an incentive for users to purchase or retain the rendered version adding markup to the rendered document without adding it to the electronic document.
    Printed Indications and “Bi-directional Markup”
    In some embodiments, rendered versions of the document contain some printed indications of the type of markup available for it. For example, words may be underlined or printed in a particular color to indicate that scanning them may result in a hyperlink action. A small icon of a movie camera may be printed alongside a paragraph in a textbook to indicate that video footage of the lecture associated with this topic is available. A dollar symbol may be printed near a reference to a book, indicating that capturing that text will initiate the purchase of the book from an online retailer.
    In some embodiments, the system adds these indications using of the markup in the process of rendering the document. Markup used this way is said to be “bi-directional,” being used both in the transition from digital to paper (printing) and from paper to digital (scanning).
    One example involves a digital XML or HTML document. Conventionally a stylesheet, such as an XSL stylesheet, is used to inform the creation of the rendered version from the XML/HTML source. This process is well-understood in the art.
    In some embodiments, the markup is available in an XML format, and the system performs an XSLT-type transformation, which draws information both from the source document and the markup to create a new XML document, which is similar to the source document but has had information added to it based on the contents of the markup. In one example, this document is identical to the source except that paragraphs that are known to have a particular type of markup associated with them have had an extra XML attribute added to their representation in the document.
    At this point, the system performs a transformation similar to that described above, involving an XSL stylesheet, on this new document to produce the rendered version afterwards, the stylesheet contains instructions that paragraphs with that particular XML attribute should be printed in blue instead of black.
    Implementation
    This section describes an implementation of the system that associates a captured phrase from a document with an online discussion relating to that part of the document.
    The user employs a hand-held scanner device to capture a few words from the rendered version of a document (for example a magazine article), and the system uses those words to identify an electronic counterpart of the rendered document (for example, an HTML version of the article from the magazine publisher's site) as described elsewhere. The system optionally retrieves this electronic counterpart and displays it to the user.
    At the same time, the system makes contact with a markup-oriented search engine and submits an HTML query containing information including the URL of the located electronic counterpart and the details of the capture, including the text scanned. In this case the user is only interested in online discussions, and the query includes information to that effect.
    The markup-oriented search engine identifies markup which is known to be associated with the URL, and examines it for references to online discussions, especially those associated with the phrase, paragraph or section of the document from which the capture occurred. The engine returns a list of all such discussions found, including the URL of the web presence of that discussion, and optionally including the headings of recent posts to the discussion. If several discussions are found, the engine returns them in order of their perceived relevance to the actual capture.
    The system presents the list of discussions to the user, such as in a pop-up menu. The user selects one and is presented with the web page on which the discussion may be viewed. If the information about particular postings to the discussion was transmitted, this may form a submenu under the menu item for the discussion. Selecting from that submenu takes the user to the actual posting concerned.
    In this way, an online discussion is associated with a section of a paper document, and a convenient means made available for the reader of the paper document to access it.

It may produce several queries, for example in cases where the content of the scan is not entirely clear. The query engine 506 performs or triggers a search on one or more indices 510 for each of the queries passed to it, and produces a set of references to the documents it find.
    The system produces an index 510 from a set of source documents 512, which may include the electronic counterpart of the rendered document from which the scan occurred. The process of creating the index starts with the gathering 514 of those source documents. In the case where those documents are available on the web, this includes the process of finding and retrieving them from their web server. In some embodiments, the system retrieves markup associated with the documents at the same time. In some embodiments, a local cache of the documents and markup 515. The system processes these gathered documents 516, for example to remove formatting instructions or to extract the basic text before being passed to the indexing process 518 which produces the index.
    In producing the set of references, the query engine 506 may take into account the real-world context in which the scan occurred using a subsystem 522 which may maintain its own database 524. For example, the geographical location of the user, if known, can be taken into account at this stage, as can information from the gathering process 514 such as the geographical location of the publisher of the documents. The query engine 506 also typically takes into account the “scan context” 532, which includes information such as information about the other scans the user has made recently, and which font and language they were in. In some embodiments, the scan context handling process 532 also maintains its own database 534.
    The references produced by the query engine 506 typically include information about the source documents 512 that are relevant to the scan. The response processing step 508 takes these references and produces output for the user. In the simplest case, this may be a list of document references from which the user may choose. More typically, it will involve the use of the  context systems  522 and 532 to determine certain aspects of the presentation, such as the prioritization of the options presented to the user or the formatting of the display.
    The response processing stage 508 may also make use of markup 542. Such markup may already have been retrieved or generated, may be retrieved or generated at the time of use, may be based on information or rules in an associated database 544. As an example, the response processing stage 508 may request from the markup handling system 542 any markup associated with the documents mentioned in the references. The markup handling system may contact the “gather” system 514 which retrieves any such markup from the original source of the documents or from its own cache. The markup handling system returns this markup to the response processing system 508, which uses it to determine the options available to the user. The response processing system may also make use of information provided by the  context handling stages  522 and 532. The system thus produces a results document and presents it to the user.
    If the user makes a selection 509 from the results document, for example to retrieve a particular document, that request may be passed to the access/billing system 552 which is responsible for retrieving said document and/or any associated data and, optionally, charging a fee for doing so. Other actions may be performed depending on the user's selection. Any results, such as the retrieved document, are presented to the user by the results processing stage 562, which may also make use of the markup handling system 542 to identify information relevant to the presentation.
